messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 30-year-old curriculum designer who came to therapy after a year of growing distress that had begun to interfere with his work. The traumatic event occurred two years ago, during a relationship with a man named Marcus, who had become increasingly controlling and volatile. One night, after Marcus had been drinking heavily, an argument escalated. Kwame remembers the sharp, sour smell of alcohol on Marcus’s breath as he was pinned against the wall, the searing pain in his ribs as he was struck repeatedly, and the terrifying sensation of hands around his throat. The apartment had a faint burnt smell from a candle that had been knocked over earlier, and that odour—mingled with alcohol—became seared into his memory. He managed to escape and ended the relationship the next day, but he never reported the abuse. He told himself it was a one-time event, and he tried to move on.

In the months that followed, Kwame found that he could not simply leave the experience behind. When he least expected it, the memory would crash over him with a force that left him breathless. He would feel the exact same physical pain in his ribs and throat, as though the blows were landing fresh, and the terror would return—the same helpless, frozen panic he had felt in that moment. Sometimes, without any apparent trigger, he would catch a smell that seemed to come from nowhere: alcohol, or that specific burnt odour from the apartment, and he would be back there, his heart pounding, his skin crawling.

The smells soon began to appear in his daily life as real, external triggers. Walking past a bar, the whiff of beer on someone’s breath would send him into a state of hypervigilance. At work—an open-plan office for an educational publishing company—a colleague once burned popcorn in the breakroom microwave, and Kwame had to excuse himself to the bathroom, shaking, for nearly twenty minutes. He began to avoid the breakroom altogether, eating lunch at his desk. He also started to dread conversations that touched on family. When a coworker asked, “So, are you close with your parents?” or someone joked about family gatherings, Kwame would feel a surge of anger and shame that he could not explain. He had come to believe that he was somehow dirty, contaminated by what had happened. The injustice of it—that Marcus had walked away without consequence, that no one knew, that nothing had been done—gnawed at him daily. He felt that the person he had become was unrecognisable: the confident, easygoing curriculum designer who once led team workshops had turned into a man who flinched at comments and avoided lunch with colleagues.

The avoidance had consequences. He stopped dating entirely, certain that any romantic partner would see the stain of his past. He turned down invitations to after-work drinks, and his supervisor noted that he seemed withdrawn and less collaborative. Kwame had always taken pride in designing inclusive, engaging learning materials, but now his creativity felt blocked. He worried that his own emotional state was affecting his work, and that he could not bring himself to write scenarios that required empathy for characters in conflict.

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment at his desk when a colleague made an offhand comment about “family drama” and Kwame felt a flash of such intense physical pain in his ribs that he gasped aloud. He realised he could no longer manage on his own. He is afraid that therapy will force him to relive the abuse, and he is ashamed that he never reported it. But he is also desperate to feel like himself again—to be able to sit through a team meeting without scanning for alcohol smells, and to believe that he is not defined by what Marcus did to him. He hopes, above all, to stop feeling dirty.
